analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy cheaper prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill to allow personal drug importation from Canada never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the FDA to set up a program letting individuals import up to a 90-day supply of prescription drugs from Canadian pharmacies approved and listed by the government. The drugs would have to match FDA-approved versions in ingredients and strength, and risky categories like controlled substances and biologics would be excluded. It was introduced in February 2021, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. prices for prescription drugs, especially those without insurance or with high out-of-pocket costs, who could buy the same drugs from Canada at prices often far lower than in the United States.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA, within 180 days of enactment, to write rules permitting individuals to safely import prescription drugs from Canada [S3].
Limits imports to a 90-day personal-use supply filled with a valid U.S. prescription, from Canadian pharmacies the Secretary certifies and publishes on an FDA website [S2][S3].

Excludes higher-risk categories — controlled substances, biological products, intravenously injected and refrigerated drugs — and requires pharmacies to run quality assurance programs with approved-laboratory product testing [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose U.S. pricing depends on keeping cheaper Canadian supplies out of the American market, and to a lesser extent U.S. pharmacies and middlemen that mark up the same drugs.

drawbacks.text: The safety chain depends on FDA certification of foreign pharmacies and product testing, and critics have long argued importation opens a channel for counterfeit or improperly stored drugs that is hard to police [S2][S3].
The bill excludes biologics, refrigerated drugs, and many advanced therapies — precisely some of the most expensive drugs — so the savings would reach only a subset of patients [S3].

Personal importation addresses individual purchases, not the underlying gap between U.S. drug prices and the prices every other wealthy country negotiates, so it does little for people who get drugs through insurance formularies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who pay cash prices, the benefit is real and immediate: the same FDA-approved drug, bought from a certified Canadian pharmacy, often at a fraction of the U.S. price. The safety concerns are legitimate but the bill answers them with certification, testing, and exclusions of the riskiest drug classes, rather than ignoring them. The main honest objection is that it is a workaround, not a fix — it lowers prices for those who use it without changing why U.S. prices are higher in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to its Health Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chellie Pingree introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, with Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler as the bill's cosponsor, making it a two-person bipartisan effort [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to that committee's Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo, in which cheaper Canadian supplies remain barred from individual importers, and U.S. patients kept paying American prices. The committee's inaction — not a vote — decided the outcome.

for.name: Rep. Chellie Pingree
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to allow personal importation of prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.

for.name: Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and the brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: Long opposed drug importation legislation and lobbied against it, arguing it threatens the drug supply and undermines patents.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill with one Republican cosponsor; no votes were ever recorded, so the wider partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: Personal importation from Canada, where drug prices are government-controlled and far lower, would let Americans buy the same drugs more cheaply, cutting into U.S. pricing power. The bill died, so the industry kept its protected U.S. market.
Certified Canadian pharmacies would have become a government-listed sales channel to U.S. patients for 90-day personal supplies. Their gain is the patient's savings on the same drug.

industries.industry: U.S. pharmacies and drug supply middlemen
industries.note: Some U.S. retail pharmacy and wholesale volume could shift to Canadian sellers. The effect is secondary to the bill's main aim of letting patients buy cheaper.
